newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch to label gene-modified food from April 1.
newsitem.headline: Dutch to label gene-modified food from April 1.

text.p: The Dutch government said on Thursday all food products made from genetically-modified soybeans must be labelled as such from April 1 next year, making it the first EU country to take a unilateral stand on the issue.
The government said it had taken the decision in collaboration with the Dutch consumers association and food industry groups in a bid to maximise transparency and freedom of choice for consumers.
"This openness will be expressed by labelling foods that contain genetically-modified material to enable the consumer to easily distinguish them from conventional foods," it said.
The label will read: "containing soya protein manufactured on the basis of modern biotechnology".
Legislation will now be drafted and is expected to be in place by April 1, pre-empting a European Union directive on the matter expected sometime next year, the government said.

"We expect a directive from Brussels on this but we suspect it will not be before mid-1997 and we didn't want to lose momentum. We will draft the legislation so that it does not conflict with Brussels," Benno Bruggink, spokesman for the Dutch public health ministry, told Reuters.

He said there were tests available to determine if soybean shipments contained genetically-altered material, and if there was any doubt over whether a food product had be made using the new beans, it would have to carry a label.
On Wednesday, the European Commission said it would soon propose improved labelling of genetically-modified foods.
"We must not miss this opportunity to repeat our clear signal that better labelling is one of the ways forward in this area," Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard said.
"The Commission intends to deal further with this problem when a proposal - as soon as possible - will be put forward for revision of (the directive)."
At present the directive does not allow obligatory labelling to show that a product is genetically modified without an assessment of the risk.
The new soybeans were developed by U.S. chemicals giant Monsanto to be resistant to its own weedkiller Roundup.

The Commission on Wednesday also approved the market release within the EU of gene-altered maize, made by Swiss chemicals company Ciba-Geigy, despite strong opposition from environmental groups. The EU said it would allow the maize to be sold in Europe subject to some labelling conditions.
